title: Definition and purpose of KISS principle

blocks.text: 8.2.1. Definition and Purpose of KISS Principle

On a Friday afternoon the shop reprices its best-selling mug from 18.99 to 21.49. Half an hour later checkout still charges 18.99, although the price cache's time to live is five minutes. The cache class is sixty lines: per-SKU entries, LRU eviction, hit counters. The pricing team's requirement is one sentence: a price shown at checkout is never more than five minutes old.

KISS ("keep it simple") asks for the simplest code that meets a stated requirement. The caches on this page are measured against that requirement written as a check, so "simple" means "passes the check with the fewest moving parts", not "short".
Expiry Counted From the Last Read Keeps a Popular Price Forever
Read `price()` and decide which SKU goes stale: the one read once an hour, or the one read every minute?

The check drives any `sku -> price` function with a fake clock (an `InstantSource`, injected as in unit 7.3.2): the mug is repriced at minute 1, read every minute to minute 30, and must show 21.49 from minute 7 on.
FAILED  PriceCache  at minute 30 shows 18.99; old price after the 5-minute limit: 24 times

Each hit writes `now` back into the entry, so the five minutes count from the last read, not from the load. A SKU read at least every five minutes is never reloaded; the one read hourly always is. The bestseller keeps the old price until reads stop at night or the service restarts.

Nobody asked for "keep hot entries alive". It is a different policy, sliding expiry, written in because general-purpose caches offer it, and it runs on every hit whether the requirement wants it or not.
One Load Time for the Whole List Meets the Requirement

The catalogue has 3,000 SKUs, and the price-list query returns all of them in a few milliseconds. So there is no need for an entry per SKU: load the whole list, record when, and reload after five minutes.

PriceList list = new PriceList(() -> new HashMap<>(catalogue), clock);   // a query returns a fresh map
check("PriceList", list::price);
ok      PriceList   at minute 30 shows 21.49; old price after the 5-minute limit: 0 times

`loadedAt` is written only when the list is loaded, so the age it measures is the age of the data. There is no eviction because 3,000 prices fit in memory, and no hit counter because nobody reads one.
The class is single-threaded as written. Shared between request threads it needs one more choice of construct, which unit 8.2.2 makes; unit 8.2.3 counts the interleavings that choice removes.
Code Simpler Than the Requirement Is a Bug, Not KISS
A one-line memo is simpler still:

Map<String, BigDecimal> memo = new HashMap<>();
check("memo", sku -> memo.computeIfAbsent(sku, catalogue::get));
FAILED  memo        at minute 30 shows 18.99; old price after the 5-minute limit: 24 times

`computeIfAbsent` calls the loader only when the key is absent, and nothing removes keys, so the first price loaded stays until the process restarts. Where `PriceCache` added a rule nobody asked for, the memo lacks the one rule that was asked for, and the check fails both.
<!-- practice 1 -->
An Option Nobody Needed Changes What Other Code May Do

`PriceCache` also evicts the least recently used SKU beyond 10,000 entries. The catalogue has 3,000, so eviction never runs, and it looks harmless. The admin page calls `report()`; its test caches one SKU and passes. Production caches two:
The program prints the exception and two of its frames:

MUG-01 18.99
java.util.ConcurrentModificationException
    at java.base/java.util.LinkedHashMap$LinkedHashIterator.nextNode(LinkedHashMap.java:1023)
    ...
    at PriceCache.report(PriceCache.java:51)

The `true` in the `LinkedHashMap` constructor turns on access order, which LRU eviction needs. In an access-ordered map `get` moves the entry it finds to the end of the order, and the javadoc counts that as a structural modification. The loop's `entries.get(sku)` reorders the map under its own iterator, and the fail-fast iterator (unit 6.5.3) throws on the next step. An entry that is already last doesn't move, so with one entry the test passed.

A Rule Engine for One Form Adds Failures the Plain Method Cannot Have

The signup form needs two checks: the email has an `@` after its first character, and the user is 18 or older. A developer who expects more forms writes a rule engine instead: rules keyed by the name of the record accessor they read, applied by reflection.
Two years later signup is still the only form. Its rules for the engine, and the same two rules written out:
public record Signup(String email, int age) {}
Both are given `new Signup("jane.example.com", 16)`. Ten runs of the same program, counted:

5 FormRules: [age, email]
      5 FormRules: [email, age]
     10 plain:     [email, age]

The engine returns violations in the map's iteration order, and `Map.of` leaves that order unspecified: here it changed from one JVM start to the next. The form shows its errors in a different order after each restart, and a test that asserts the list passes on some runs and fails on others.

Then the record component is renamed to `contactEmail`. An IDE rename refactoring updates Java references, so it updates `s.email()` too; a string literal changes only if you also ask it to search text and accept that occurrence. Renamed by hand in `Signup.java`, the plain version no longer compiles:

SignupCheck.java:15: error: cannot find symbol
        if (s.email().indexOf('@') <= 0) failed.add("email");
             ^
  symbol:   method email()
  location: variable s of type Signup
1 error
Either way, a program that uses only the engine (`EngineCheck`, its `main` validating the same signup) compiles cleanly, and the first signup fails:

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.IllegalStateException: cannot read email
	at FormRules.violations(FormRules.java:15)
	at EngineCheck.main(EngineCheck.java:10)
Caused by: java.lang.NoSuchMethodException: Signup.email()
	at java.base/java.lang.Class.getMethod(Class.java:2397)
	at FormRules.violations(FormRules.java:12)
	... 1 more
The engine turned two method calls into strings, and javac checks no strings. When to share code between forms that do exist is unit 8.3.4's subject.
The Plain Version Fits Today's Numbers; When They Change, Replace It

`PriceList` is simple because the list loads fast. Then the catalogue grows. Here is how long each checkout's `price()` takes, one checkout a minute, with the query replaced by building a map of that many entries (one machine, Java 21):

3,000 SKUs, ms per checkout, one a minute: 5 0 0 0 0 3 0 0 0 0 1
 2,000,000 SKUs, ms per checkout, one a minute: 1105 0 0 0 0 1142 0 0 0 0 1293

At two million SKUs the first checkout after each five-minute mark waits over a second. If a requirement says no checkout waits, the next design reloads in the background and swaps the new map in (unit 8.2.2), with a check of its own for that requirement.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **Expiry counted from the last read keeps a popular price forever.** A general-purpose cache brings rules of its own, and sliding expiry broke "never more than five minutes old" for the SKU read most.
**One load time for the whole list meets the requirement.** With 3,000 SKUs that load in milliseconds, a map and a timestamp written only on load pass the check.
**Code simpler than the requirement is a bug.** A `computeIfAbsent` memo never reloads and fails the same check.
**An option nobody needed changes what other code may do.** Access order, turned on for eviction that never runs, makes `get` a structural modification, and the report throws CME with two SKUs.
**A rule engine for one form adds failures the plain method cannot have.** Its order changes between runs, and a renamed accessor compiles and fails at the first signup.
**The plain version fits today's numbers.** At two million SKUs one checkout every five minutes waits a second; the replacement is written when that requirement exists.

blocks.text: Challenges

items: The pricing team adds a rule: a price changed by hand in the back office shows at checkout within ten seconds. Which of the three designs on this page survives, and what is the simplest change that meets the new requirement?
Your service already has a cache library on the classpath, with expiry after write as an option. Is configuring it simpler than `PriceList`? Count the rules each one brings.
Find a class in your codebase with an option set "in case": a pool size, a retry policy, an eviction limit. What does it change about the code around it today?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why the Check Comes Before the Code

"Simple" has no measure on its own. The `computeIfAbsent` memo has fewer lines and branches than `PriceList` and fails the check; `PriceCache` handles more situations than either and fails it too. Written first, the requirement's check turns "simplest" into a question with an answer: the least code that passes it.

The cost is that the plain design is chosen for today's numbers and replaced, not extended, when they change. The alternative is a general design on day one, which carries rules nobody requested (sliding expiry, access order, string-keyed rules) from the start, each with behaviour no check was written for.
